how-much-should-a-wedding-dj-charge.html.text:
DJ Gig Profit Calculator · GUIDE

How much should a wedding DJ charge?

Worked on invented numbers; put yours into the quote builder. Nothing here is a market price.

One reception, priced from the bottom up

A 5-hour reception quoted at $1,200. Around it: 2 hours of load-in and load-out, 2 hours of planning and music prep, 1 hour of driving. That is 5 unpaid hours on top of 5 playing hours, 10 hours of work, and 50% of it is not on the dance floor.

LineAmount
Quote price$1,200.00
Card fee (3%)$36.00
Gear wear ($6,000 over 150 gigs)$40.00
Insurance share ($600 over 60 gigs)$10.00
Software share ($900 over 60 gigs)$15.00
Mileage (40 miles at $0.70)$28.00
Take-home profit$1,071.00

Profit divided by 10 hours is $107.10 per hour worked, against $240.00 per playing hour on the quote. The break-even price, where profit is zero and your 10 hours are unpaid, is $96; the price that pays $60 per hour worked is $714. Overtime should be billed at no less than $61.86 per hour to cover the same target.

Deposit schedule

Deposit at booking: $360.00; Balance due 14 days before the event: $840.00.

Good, better, best

Each tier is priced from its own hours and costs at the same $60 per hour target, rounded up to $25. Add-ons: ceremony sound (good), cocktail hour and uplighting (better), photo booth and MC (best).

TierHours workedPriceProfitPer hour
good10.5$775$644$61.31
better12$925$739$61.60
best12.5$1,100$759$60.72

Pricing a year

To take home $60,000 over 60 gigs, 35 in peak season and 25 off-season with peak priced 20% higher, the base package needs about $1,009 off-season and $1,211 at peak. That is 600 hours of work a year and $100.00 per hour worked.

Common questions

How much should a wedding DJ charge?

Work from the hours you really spend. On the example numbers a 5-hour reception costs 10 hours of work once 5 unpaid hours of load-in, planning and driving are added, so a $1,200 quote is $240.00 per playing hour but $107.10 per hour worked. Local prices differ; enter your own figures in the calculator.

What is the break-even price for a DJ gig?

The price at which take-home profit is zero: your gig costs divided by one minus the fees. On the example it is $96, and the price that pays $60 per hour worked is $714.

How do I price a year, not a gig?

Pick the take-home you want, then solve for the price. To take home $60,000 over 60 gigs (35 peak, 25 off-season, peak 20% higher) the example needs about $1,009 off-season and $1,211 at peak.

Is this advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, not tax, legal or financial advice, and it does not know what weddings cost in your town.

Your business

Event hours are the hours you play; setup, travel, teardown and planning hours are added to every gig. Overhead is spread over the hours you can work, not the hours you fill. Gigs per month are converted to a weekly mix using your weeks per year.

How it is calculated

Slot: event hours plus setup and planning hours. Overhead per hour: monthly overhead × 12 ÷ (hours per week × weeks per year). Contribution: price × (1 − card fee) − gig costs. Profit per hour: contribution ÷ slot hours − overhead per hour. Price for target: ((target + overhead per hour) × slot hours + gig costs) ÷ (1 − card fee). Lead marketplace: price × (1 − lead fee), then the same costs and overhead. Agency: your share of price plus tips, less gig costs and the share of overhead you still carry.

Not modelled: payroll and self-employment tax, sales tax, deposits and cancellations, overtime clauses, the extra bookings a marketplace or agency may bring, seasonality, and local market prices. Unverified: tested on hand-calculated examples, not against a real DJ's books.

Common questions

How much should a DJ charge for a wedding?

Work backwards from the hours. Add the event hours to setup, travel and consultation time, multiply by the hourly take-home you want plus your overhead per working hour, add the gig's own costs such as fuel, a helper and lighting rental, then divide by one minus your card fee. That is the price floor. This tool does the arithmetic from your own figures; it does not know what weddings cost in your town.

Why does setup and travel time matter so much?

A five-hour reception is rarely five hours of work. Load-in, soundcheck, travel, teardown and planning calls often double the time, so an hourly rate quoted on event hours alone overstates what you earn per hour worked. Enter your real setup and prep hours and the table shows profit per hour worked.

What should go in monthly overhead?

Gear replacement set-aside, insurance, music pool and software subscriptions, website, vehicle costs not tied to one gig, storage and marketing. Overhead is spread over the hours you can work each week, not the hours you happen to fill.

Is a lead marketplace or an agency worth it?

The tool replays your monthly mix three ways: direct clients, a lead marketplace that takes a percentage of each booked gig, and subcontracting for an agency that keeps part of the price. It compares weekly income and income per hour worked. It does not value the extra bookings a marketplace or agency might send you, so compare the result with how many more gigs you expect.

Is a price raise worth the clients I might lose?

The raise table shows the share of gigs you could lose before a price rise costs you money. Overhead does not shrink when clients leave, so the break-even loss is the extra revenue divided by the new total contribution.

Does it include tips?

Enter a tip percentage and it adds tips to the model comparison. Tips are not included in the price floor.

Is my information uploaded?

No. The calculation runs in your browser from figures you type, nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and it works offline after the page loads. No client or event details are needed or accepted.
